By putting thoughts into the written word. The world still needs humans who can think great thoughts and put them in writing all by themselves. Relegating writing to nothing but a chore to be eliminated is a value judgment, not a widely accepted fact.

comments.name: SP
comments.body:
Bret Stephens is right that something in writing must be effortful. He is wrong about which part.

Consider retyping Moby Dick. Every keystroke mine, months of labor, no machine involved — and I would not have written a word of it. Now consider a man who cannot type, who dictates a letter and revises it eleven times until it says what he means. He wrote it. Physical effort is not the variable. Judgment is: whether anything was chosen, rejected, and chosen again.
His own example gives it away. The bride is insulted because she found out — undisclosed substitution in a form where personal composition is expected. That is the deception problem he set aside in his third paragraph as solvable. No president credits his speechwriter mid-address, and nobody claims Kennedy's judgment suffered for it.

I am writing books with AI's help. Chapters went from version one to version forty-five. That is not accepting what a machine produced; it is rejecting it, repeatedly, until the page says what happened. A model can ask better questions about the rooms I sat in. It cannot furnish them.

The failure he fears is real. It comes from ceasing to be the one who discriminates — which can happen with a machine, with a ghostwriter, or alone at a desk with a notepad and no standards.

The instruction is not never use it. It is stay the one who chooses.

comments.name: Stephen Klinger
comments.body: Mr. Stephens is correct regarding the vast majority of students and semi-literate adults who are increasingly using AI as a thinking and communicating crutch, so I agree with his motive and broad advice—but not his absolutism. As many of these comments point out, judicious and restrained use of AI on certain writing tasks and collaborations does not invariably erode the word-formulation process or inevitably atrophy the mind muscle of those who use it with self-awareness, restraint and defined purpose. For the few, it can foster clearer thinking and become a learning experience. For the many, it is as Mr. Stephens describes it. I never use AI to write or copy-edit, but sometimes to critique what I have written or quickly research points of information. I also, when necessary, shop at Walmart.

comments.name: Manufactured Reality
comments.body: Poppycock Mr. Stephens. This reminds me of the schoolmarms in the 60’s protesting calculators. Clutching your pearls won’t help here. Yes, you can use AI as a crutch. Yes, it can take agency away from people who might not like to write anyway. Yes, AI is going to be used by cheaters, bad actors, and uninspired students. It’s a very complex subject. It’s not just a question of never use it. That is way too simplistic. There is a thing called COLLABORATION. It’s when you collaborate with a thing. It’s not just a binary. I have found AI to be a great tool to bounce ideas off of, clarify thinking, play devils advocate, create super useful functional code, and yes even learn from. I understand the knee jerk reaction coming from a conservative columnist. To be conservative generally means you want to preserve the status quo, and in some things it’s important to conserve. But, the alien is here whether we like it or not. The real enemy is capital. Those in charge and in possession of huge amounts of capital are going to use AI to consolidate power and exert control for maximum profit. If by some miracle the humans could see beyond late stage capitalism, we could work on alignment. AI’s aligned with human flourishing could be a key to our collective survival. Yes, it does not look good right now for the humans, but that is not the fault of the AI’s.

comments.name: Matthew Berg
comments.body:
I've spent a few hundred dollars on Whatnot, and it's fascinating to watch people spend thousands of dollars on sports cards with as little as 10 seconds to make a decision.

For certain buyers, especially sports card shop owners and experienced dealers, Whatnot has a clear advantage. They often know market values well enough to set a maximum bid that still leaves room for profit when the card becomes inventory in their shop.

For many buyers, though, it's a different story. Without a strong understanding of current market values, it's easy to overpay in the excitement of a live auction. The fast-paced format leaves very little time to research comparable sales or make an informed decision.

That's where eBay has a significant advantage. Auctions typically last several days, giving buyers time to research recent sales, compare prices, and determine a fair value before placing a bid. Sellers also provide multiple high-resolution photos, making it much easier to evaluate centering, corners, edges, surface condition, and other details that can dramatically affect a card's value. During a live stream, especially with only a few seconds to bid, it's difficult to examine those same details with confidence.

Whatnot is undeniably entertaining, and for knowledgeable buyers it can be a great platform. But for the average collector, the speed and excitement of live auctions can sometimes lead to purchases that aren't as well-informed as they would be on a platform like eBay.

Small regional business are thus able to access the sort of mass-distribution networks that were hitherto the preserve of the likes of Walmart.

Of course there will be a tiny number of customers who get "amped-up" by the auction process itself, but surely that does not mean that regulators should shut off opportunities to emerging entrepreneurs with real good sand services to sell. The time of the impact has passed.

Computer simulations considered the rocket stage coming down in a vertical orientation, which would produce the most debris, but the stage could have easily bellyflopped at an angle instead. Observations from telescopes on Earth could take hours or days of analysis to reveal minuscule hints. They could come up empty, too.

The Korean spacecraft Danuri will pass over the site about eight hours after impact (about 10:35 a.m. Eastern time). Even if it successfully captures an image of where the crash occurred, it could take days or weeks to identify it. 

The process is like finding a needle in a haystack, and the only way you can confirm there's a new needle (crater) is by comparing it with an earlier photograph that shows that the surface at that location was previously pristine.

NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter will pass over the site in six days.

Is it at all possible that the predictions were wrong, and the rocket stage actually missed? 

No, not unless aliens were able to push it out of the way of the moon. 

Like everything flying around in the solar system, the motion of a rocket stage followed Newton's laws of motion with only slight deviations from additional forces like the solar wind. The uncertainty in where the impact would occur was just a few miles.

READ AT YOUR OWN RISK. 
*Not recommended by 1 in 10 dentists.*

I have had depression for most of my life. People with depression often struggle with is basic self-care. Many nights I just can’t muster the energy to brush my teeth. It’s hard to believe if you haven’t been there — and easy to understand if you have. 

A while ago I lost my job and money was tight. A friend invited me to lunch to cheer me up. I explained that I will order only what I can pay for. We split the tab. 

That friend is funny, smart and hard-working. We began to see a lot of each other. I have shared my struggles with her in many phone calls. Recently, she said “I can easily imagine a future with you but we need to talk about personal appearance and its impact on attraction, personal life, and professional advancement...”

I asked “Is this about the enormous black head behind your ear?” Suddenly I could hear her mother cackling in the background. I asked if I was on speaker-phone. Her mother was laughing so hard she could barely breathe.

Later she told me that she really wanted to talk about my teeth. I knew exactly what she meant and was not offended. 

So I went to an oral surgeon who fitted me for veneers. I look and feel better than I have in decades. But dental work is expensive

comments.name: Glenn Koenig
comments.body:
Gosh, Finland has a population smaller than the state of Massachusetts!  The United States has 57 times more people than Finland. That makes reaching a national consensus here likely to be 57 times more difficult than it is there.

And schools?  Our model of only teaching children is based on the old assumption that schools give you everything needed to prepare for life as an adult. This is absurd in a world now changing as rapidly as it is. By the time you get a passing grade at something in the classroom, half of it is already obsolete.

Finally, let’s look at the truly big picture. We have come to depend on hugely complex supply chains for almost everything by now, including food, consumer goods, and information. As a result we cannot see or evaluate what’s being done to make and deliver all that to us. This is a giant overreach, but it has evolved for centuries by now, so most of us haven’t really noticed.

Now AI is positioned to destroy our reliance on information from unseen sources. We are now being forced to work with each other face to face, locally, where trust is not perfect, but deep fakes are a lot less likely.  We must transition to local sources for food and goods as much as possible. This way, we can see first hand how things are grown, processed, and made. We are being forced to reduce our reliance on giant government and business institutions as they have become unmanageable and often corrupt. This is everyone’s curriculum now, not just for children.

Now that Russia is hitting back, this strategy doesn't look quite so clever. Taking a step or two back, we can try to assess the overall significance of this "tit for tat" approach. It becomes apparent that even when Ukraine manages to make headlines with a photogenic assault on some Russian target, the picture remains grim. Ukraine's economy continues to decline. Its prospects for getting through another winter with a profoundly damaged electrical grid and disruptions in fuel supplies aren't looking good. Russia's blockade of Odessa and other ports is rapidly depriving it of access to the sea. Its population has plunged. Its young men are fleeing conscription. The Zelensky government is rocked by corruption scandals. Why is this unwinnable war being prolonged? It's long past time to strike a peace deal, something wanted by a majority of Ukrainians according to recent polling.

A wonderful life, thank you Mr. Pepe for inspiration.

As young marrieds in 1973 and 1974 my wife, Madolyn, and I were lucky enough to live in Italy. On weekends and holidays we would load our young son into our Fiat 150 and go someplace new - on a budget, no car seat and no seat belts. During that time we saw and fell in love with most of northern and Central Italy. In subsequent years our family, now adding our daughter and sometimes in-laws and friends, made many, many trips to Italy.

One trip I remember like it was yesterday was our little family's first voyage to Tuscany. Just before lunch we saw a small vineyard and farm on a back road in the Chianti Classico region with a bottle of wine on a pillar at the opening of the farm's driveway. The 'sign' that their wine was for sale.

The farmer greeted us and showed us around. We sampled some of their wine and he introduced us to 'Vin Santo'. He was very proud of their production. 

We bought a few cases of Chianti and one of Vin Santo. We were then asked to join the family for lunch.

The Nonna took our two year old by the hand. They came back with two home raised squab they had taken, killed and plucked - part of the ensuing meal. Our boy held one up and said, "Mama, Cena"

We had a few hours outside eating, drinking and talking - our rudimentary Italian worked well enough.

My wife passed on two years ago and this story reminded me of her and the many, many happy days we had in Italy. Thank you NYT and the Pepe family.

The whites are described as "beautifully textured and saline". Is salinity ("saltiness") a desirable quality in wines? (A little salt makes lemonade more refreshing on a hot day, but a pricey wine isn't typically consumed as a thirst-quencher.)

The 4-year wines are described as "tight and austere, their nuances locked behind a wall of tannins." 
1. I'm unsure what "tightness"  refers to in a wine (though in a  person, it refers to drunkenness). Similarly. "austerity" in a wine, referring to high acidity and tannin content, is usually not considered a good thing, anymore than in an economy. 
2. "Wall of tannins" would, in a much cheaper wine, indicate undrinkability due to excessive astringency, and the need for more aging . While tannins - natural antioxidants and antimicrobials, present in both grape seeds and oak barrels- contribute desirable flavor, they need sufficient time to do so: aging polymerizes and oxidizes the tannin molecules, mellowing their taste by reducing bitterness and astringency.
 (In a "Rumpole of the Bailey" short story, "Rumpole and the Wine Tasting", a wine critic describes a cheap and particularly vile, super-astringent brand of wine by saying that "Serving it would be considered infanticide".)

comments.name: jk
comments.body:
Strict rules around ABA therapy simply won’t work. The needs of these clients are idiosyncratic and shift rapidly as skills change, kids mature, their experiences change, and so on. But the ABA method itself is self- correcting: the practitioner collects data throughout each session; the results are analyzed (note the 2nd “A” in ABA), and the program is regularly adjusted toward reaching the defined goals of the specific program for the specific child. It’s the funding system of insurance payments creating the problems. 

ABA isn’t a “racket”. It is labor-intensive, and until the last decade, there weren’t enough practitioners. Why? Only wealthy families, or parents who could drain their retirement accounts, or mortgage their homes could pay for it. Only when health insurers were required to provide ABA did the case numbers explode. Case in point: Washington State health insurers were required to cover ABA in 2012, and the first ABA service provider arrived in  Olympia. 

For ABA to be worth its cost, it has to be individualized in form and content, carefully monitored by qualified staff, and frequently adjusted, stopped, restarted, increased and decreased, as the data collected in sessions dictate.

For many kids, ABA is THE only effective treatment that will mitigate the disabling aspects of the condition.  ABA therapy is self-correcting. More rules and scrutiny by inexpert regulators will make ABA ineffective, wasteful, and harm the people with autism who need the help.

The other 90% or so have structural issues ranging from concerning to hazardous to perilous. Finding those problems can be time-consuming and messy as they are typically behind walls, above ceilings or are otherwise encased. Further, it often involves assembling original plans and all subsequent renovation plans and may involve lab testing of materials like concrete, reinforcing steel and structural steel to be certain contractors used the type intended by the designers. The risk is that this shift concentrates their customer base in a small number of large buyers, which can weaken pricing power if those customers have significant bargaining leverage. It can also make revenue less stable because a few major contracts or purchasing decisions may have an outsized effect on overall sales. For investors, this kind of dependence can raise expectations for rapid AI-driven growth while also increasing concern about volatility if demand from those customers slows or shifts. Like so many other reasons and examples, this goes to show the perversity ingrained in our private health care system. Why can't we be like EVERY other advanced nation and have national health care (i.e., removing the excessive administrative costs and the profit margins)?
